corrected_value.title: Lexical acquisition and the modular lexicon.

decisions.quote:
In this final experiment, a more powerful test of the episodic L2

hypothesis is carried out using a more robust form of priming,

namely, repetition priming rather than translation priming. As

explained earlier, it has been found that in an episodic recognition

task, old words show strong masked repetition priming, but there

is no priming for new words (Forster, 1985; Rajaram & Neely,

1992). This result was obtained with native English speakers, so
the priming is L1–L1. The interpretation was that priming in this

task must be restricted to words that were represented episodically.

If there is no episodic representation, then there is nothing to be

primed, other than the lexical representation, which is irrelevant to

decision making in this task. What might be expected for L2

speakers of English, then? If their L2 English words are already

stored episodically (whether studied or not), then repetition prim-
ing should be observed regardless of whether the words were old

or new. This should not be the case for native speakers of English,

who should show priming only for old items.
decisions.location: Experiment 3 Introduction, p. 8 (and Introduction, p. 2; Experiment 3 Results and Discussion, p. 9, Table 4; References, p. 12)
decisions.reason: Witzel and Forster (2012) Experiment 3 empirically re-tests the specific prior finding of Forster (1985) that in an episodic recognition task, native English speakers exhibit masked repetition priming only for studied ('old') words and not for unstudied foil ('new') words. Experiment 3 collects new masked repetition priming data in an episodic recognition task from 24 native English speakers alongside 20 Chinese-English bilinguals (p. 8; Table 4, p. 9), finding significant priming in native English speakers for old English words (48 ms, t = 7.42, p = .0001) and no significant priming for new English words (4 ms, t = 1.11, p = .28), and explicitly compares these native speaker results against Forster (1985) in the Experiment 3 Discussion (p. 9). Addressing the prior pilot objection regarding background citations vs. empirically retested baselines, the L1 native-speaker comparison group in Experiment 3 is not mere background motivation or method reuse, because the old-only priming dissociation in native speakers is empirically tested in a new sample and evaluated against Forster (1985). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 677: Jiang & Forster, 2001, doi:10.1006/jmla.2000.2737, 'Cross-language priming asymmetries in lexical decision and episodic recognition') is a different original study on bilingual L2-L1 translation priming retested in Experiment 1 (matched to target_index 0). Sibling missing target_index 2 (Rajaram & Neely, 1992, doi:10.1016/0749-596X(92)90009-M) is an independent study in Journal of Memory and Language rather than an alternate or preliminary report of Forster (1985).

corrected_value.title: Dissociative masked repetition priming and word frequency effects in lexical decision and episodic recognition tasks.

decisions.quote:
That Chinese–English bilinguals show repetition priming for
both old and new L2 items in episodic recognition is a novel and

potentially important finding. However, it might be argued that

masked repetition priming is such a robust effect that it can be

obtained in any task with any population, and therefore the inter-

pretation rests entirely on the failure to find repetition priming for

new words with the monolingual English speakers (see Table 4).

However, this finding has been observed at least twice before
(Forster, 1985; Rajaram & Neely, 1992) and hence must be treated

as a reliable phenomenon.
decisions.location: Experiment 3 Discussion, p. 9 (and Introduction, p. 2; Experiment 3 Introduction, p. 8; Table 4, p. 9; References, p. 13)
decisions.reason: Witzel and Forster (2012) Experiment 3 jointly cites and empirically re-tests Rajaram and Neely (1992) alongside Forster (1985) for the specific empirical finding that native English speakers in an episodic recognition task show masked repetition priming only for studied ('old') words and not for unstudied ('new') foil words (p. 2, p. 8, p. 9). Experiment 3 tests 24 native English speakers on studied and unstudied English words in episodic recognition with masked repetition primes (Table 4, p. 9: 48 ms priming for old words, p = .0001; 4 ms for new words, p = .28) and explicitly states in the Experiment 3 Discussion (p. 9) that the failure to find repetition priming for new words with monolingual English speakers replicates the phenomenon observed in Forster (1985) and Rajaram and Neely (1992). Addressing the prior pilot objection, this is an explicit empirical retest of the baseline native-speaker dissociation in Results/Discussion rather than mere background or task borrowing. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 677: Jiang & Forster, 2001, doi:10.1006/jmla.2000.2737) is a distinct bilingual translation-priming study retested in Experiment 1 (target_index 0), and sibling target_index 1 (Forster, 1985, doi:10.1080/01690968508402073) is a separate independent publication by different authors in Language and Cognitive Processes, so report equivalence does not apply.

decisions.quote: Replication. The primary target of replication was the relationship between political ideology and the binding foundations. In the aggregate sample (N = 6,966), items that emphasized concerns for the in-group, authority, or purity were deemed more relevant for moral judgment by the political right than by the political left (r = .14, p = 6.05e -34 , d = 0.29, 95% CI = [0.25, 0.34], q = 0.15, 95% CI = [0.12, 0.17]). This result is consistent with the hypothesis that binding foundations are perceived as more morally relevant by members of the political right than by members of the political left. The overall effect size was smaller than the original (d = 0.29, 95% CI = [0.25, 0.34], vs. original d = 0.52).

corrected_value.title: Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning

decisions.quote: In the aggregate replication sample (N = 7,396), participants who were asked "which group the target object belongs to" were more likely to classify on the basis of a rule (M = 64%, SD = 25%) than on the basis of family resemblance (M = 36%, SD = 25%), and participants who were asked "which group the target object is more similar to" were more likely to classify on the basis of family resemblance (M = 56%, SD = 21%) than on the basis of a rule (M = 44%, SD = 21%). The likelihood of using a rule was higher in the belong-to condition compared with the similar-to condition, t(7227.59) = 37.05, p = 3.04e -275 , d = 0.86, 95% CI = [0.81, 0.91]. This pattern was in the same direction as the original aggregate result, and the effect size was somewhat larger: People were more likely to categorize on the basis of a rule when they considered what group the target belonged to and more likely to categorize on the basis of family resemblance when they considered what group the target was similar to.

corrected_value.title: How Elastic Are Preferences for Redistribution? Evidence from Randomized Survey Experiments.

decisions.quote:
The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. In section I, we repli-
cate past ﬁndings on the ﬂat trend in overall redistributive demand in the
United States over the past several decades, and we establish new facts
on heterogeneity by demographic subgroup. In section II, we explore how
effectively standard models explain these divergent subgroup results. In
section III, we explore hypotheses speciﬁc to the elderly, and in section IV
we do the same for blacks. In section V, we offer concluding thoughts and
suggest areas for future work.


I. Trends in Redistributive Demand
While aggregate demand for redistribution has not increased over this period
of rising inequality, in this section we document substantial heterogeneity
in this pattern across subgroups. To ensure that our heterogeneous patterns
are not driven by data or coding differences between our paper and previ-
ous work, we ﬁrst demonstrate that we can replicate the earlier ﬁnding of
ﬂat aggregate demand using our survey measures.
decisions.location: Introduction and Section I ('Trends in Redistributive Demand'), pp. 368, 371-375, Figure 2 (and References, p. 404)
decisions.reason: Ashok, Kuziemko, and Washington (2015) explicitly state in the Introduction (p. 368) that U.S. demand for redistribution has remained flat by some measures and decreased according to others ('see Kuziemko and others 2013') and state in the Introduction (pp. 368, 371) and Section I / I.A (pp. 371-375, Figure 2) that they first replicate the earlier finding of flat or slightly negative aggregate U.S. redistributive demand over the past several decades across four survey questions and two data sets (GSS and ANES). Addressing the prior pilot objection, Section I.A carries out an explicit empirical replication in Results rather than mere background motivation. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2155: Kenworthy & McCall, 2007/2008, doi:10.1093/ser/mwm006, 'Inequality, public opinion and redistribution') is a distinct cross-national eight-country study in Socio-Economic Review by different authors (matched to target_index 1), not an alternate report of Kuziemko, Norton, Saez, and Stantcheva (2013, NBER Working Paper no. 18865; revised 2015 in American Economic Review). corrected_value.title: Career mobility, job match, and overeducation

decisions.quote:
4.3    Testing for Robustness: Access to On-the-Job Training

Finally, we test the results obtained in the previous step for robustness, analysing on-

the-job training activities for under- and overeducated workers. This is done using

two indicators, a subjective and an objective one. First, we use the respondents’

answers to the question: “Do you feel that, when doing your job, you are always

learning things that could lead to a better job or promotion?” (response alternatives:

“absolutely correct,” “partly correct,” “not correct”). This question was posed in the

GSOEP in the years 1985, 1987, 1989, and 1997. Robst (1995) used the same

question and concluded for the United States that, contrary to the career mobility

hypothesis, overeducated workers are no more likely to acquire knowledge that could

lead to a better job. Second, we use information gathered in the years 1989 and 1993

on whether GSOEP respondents had participated in a job-related training measure

lasting more than one day in the preceding three-year period (“yes” or “no”).
decisions.location: Section 4.3 ('Testing for Robustness: Access to On-the-Job Training'), pp. 16-17, Tables 5 and 6 (and Abstract; Introduction, pp. 2-3; References, p. 22)
decisions.reason: Beyond citing Robst (1995) in the Abstract and Introduction (p. 2), Büchel and Mertens (2001/2004) explicitly re-test Robst's (1995) empirical finding on overeducation/undereducation and on-the-job training in Section 4.3 (pp. 16-17, Tables 5 and 6) using West German GSOEP panel data (1984-1997). In Section 4.3, they first replicate Robst's (1995) subjective training measure using the identical survey question on whether the respondent's job involves learning new things, and second test an objective measure of formal on-the-job training in the 1989 and 1993 waves, concluding in the Introduction (p. 3) and Section 4.3 (pp. 16-17) that both specifications confirm Robst's (1995) findings for the U.S. that overeducated workers receive less training and undereducated workers receive more training than correctly allocated workers. Addressing the prior pilot objection, Section 4.3 is an explicit empirical retest in Results rather than mere background discussion. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 322: Sicherman, 1991, doi:10.1086/298261, 'Overeducation in the Labor Market', Journal of Labor Economics) is a distinct original paper retested in Section 4.1 (matched to target_index 0), not an alternate report of Robst (1995, Eastern Economic Journal, 21, 539-550). No DOI is printed for Robst (1995) in the source text, so doi is omitted.
